Lesson 01

Call an API without putting the key in the repo

Why it matters

The key lives in an environment or a secret store. The client reads it at runtime. Logs do not print it.

Try it: Guardrail sandbox

Lesson
01 of 07
Time
12 min
Level
Core
Lives in
Environment or secret store
Loaded
At runtime
Logs
Must not print it

A hosted model is a metered remote service. The API key is a password that spends money and may be tied to your data-retention settings. Treat it that way.

  1. Create a key with the minimum scope and a spend cap if the provider offers one.
  2. Put it in an environment variable or a secret manager. Do not put it in a source file, a notebook that you will commit, or a screenshot.
  3. Add the env file to your ignore rules before the first run, not after the leak.
  4. Use a separate key for experiments and for anything shared.
  5. If a key appears in a chat, a log, or a ticket, revoke it. Do not 'be more careful next time' with the same key.
export MODEL_API_KEY=...   # in a shell profile or a secret store, not in git
# client reads os.environ['MODEL_API_KEY']
# log the model id and the status code, never the Authorization header

Practice

Write the three places your key must never appear: a filename, a log field, and a chat surface you actually use. If you do not have a key, write the rule anyway.

Check

What do you do if a key lands in a log?

Show the answer

Revoke it, then fix the log. Keeping the key and editing one file is not enough if the log was copied.

Lesson 02

Ask for structured output and check it

Why it matters

Schema mode is a feature of the API. Your parser is still the gate.

Try it: Function-call check

Hosted APIs in 2026 generally offer a way to constrain output: JSON schema, tool definitions, or a response format flag. Use it for anything a program will read. Then parse and validate. On failure, record the raw body, retry once with the validator message, and stop.

Structured output does not make the values true. A schema can require source_id to be a string and still receive an id you do not have. Check membership against the ids you sent.

CheckWhere
Parseable, required keys presentYour code, after the call.
Enum values are in the allowed setYour code.
Ids were in the inputYour code, against the request.
The prose is kindNot a parse check. Put it in an eval if you care.

Practice

List the three checks you would run on the decision schema from the prompting track. Mark which ones a JSON schema cannot do alone.

Check

What can a schema guarantee?

Show the answer

Shape. Not truth, and not that an id exists in your corpus.

Lesson 03

Set timeouts, retries, and a rate-limit plan

Why it matters

A hung call is a product bug. A retry storm is a bill.

Try it: Cost and latency

Lesson
03 of 07
Time
10 min
Level
Practice
Timeout
A product limit
Retries
A small budget
Storm
A bill

Every client needs a timeout. Choose it from the user's patience, not from hope. A chat answer and an overnight batch do not share a timeout.

  • Retry transient failures: network errors, 429, and 5xx, with backoff and a small cap.
  • Do not retry 400 errors caused by a bad request. Fix the request.
  • Do not retry a tool that already charged a card or sent a message. Those need an idempotency key, which School 06 covers.
  • When the provider says to wait, wait. A loop that immediately retries is how you extend an outage and the invoice.

Timeouts also bound runaway reasoning models. If the product cannot wait, do not call a model that might think for a minute. Fall back or tell the person the job is still running.

Practice

For a task you have in mind, write the timeout, the maximum retries, and one error you will not retry.

Check

Why is an immediate retry of a 429 a mistake?

Show the answer

The provider asked you to slow down. Immediate retries spend the same quota faster and can make the block longer.

Lesson 04

Read the bill in tokens, cache, and batch

Why it matters

Cost is a property of the design. Input tokens, output tokens, and tool calls are the levers.

Try it: Cost and latency

Lesson
04 of 07
Time
12 min
Level
Core
Levers
Input, output, cache, tools
Unit
Per successful task
Prices
Read the card

Most hosted prices are per token, with input cheaper than output, and with extra rates for reasoning tokens, large context, or specialized tools. Read the current price page when you estimate. Do not memorize a number from this course.

Levers that actually move the bill

  • Send fewer input tokens: retrieve a passage instead of the corpus.
  • Cap output tokens to what the schema needs.
  • Use prompt caching when the same long prefix is reused. Measure the hit, do not assume it.
  • Batch work that is not interactive. Batches are often cheaper and always slower.
  • Route easy rows to a smaller model. The router is only worth it if the eval says the small model passes those rows.

Track cost per successful task, not cost per call. A cheap call that fails and gets retried by a person is not cheap.

Practice

Sketch a one-line estimate: input tokens, output cap, and number of calls for one successful task. Leave the currency blank until you read the price page, and write the date you will check it.

Check

Why is cost per call the wrong product number?

Show the answer

Because failed calls, retries, and human cleanup are part of the real cost of a successful task.

Lesson 05

Compare providers on the same ten tasks

Why it matters

Swap the client. Keep the fixture, the schema, and the scorecard.

Try it: Cost and latency

A provider comparison is an eval with more than one client. The tasks, the expected checks, and the recorded fields stay identical: quality, safety fails, latency, and cost. Changing the prompt to flatter one provider invalidates the comparison.

Also record the operational facts: data-retention default, region, whether prompt caching exists, and how structured output is spelled in that API. A model that scores well and retains data you cannot retain is not a win.

Multi-provider is a maintenance cost

Two clients means two schemas, two failure modes, and two invoices. Take that on when the eval or the constraint demands it, not because an architecture diagram had a second box.

Practice

Write the header row of a comparison sheet: provider, model id, pass count, safety fails, median latency, cost for the ten, retention note. Fill 'not run' if you have not called anyone.

Check

What must stay constant when you swap providers?

Show the answer

The tasks, the checks, and the fields you record. Otherwise you are comparing prompts, not providers.

Lesson 06

Log the call without logging the secret

Why it matters

Keep the model id, the latency, the token counts, and a hash or id of the prompt. Drop the key and the raw private text unless you have a place to store it.

Try it: Guardrail sandbox

You will need logs when a call fails. You do not need the Authorization header, and you often do not need the full prompt if the prompt contains private text. Design the log line before the first incident.

Log thisDo not log this
Timestamp, model id, status, latency, token countsAPI keys, bearer tokens, cookies
A prompt id or hash, and the fixture idRaw customer documents, unless the log store is approved for them
Validator errorsThe contents of a .env file

Staging and production keys differ. A log from staging should be obvious, so a debug session does not 'just this once' use the production key against a toy prompt that contains real data.

Practice

Write one log line, with fake values, that would be safe to paste into a ticket. Then write the same event the unsafe way, and cross it out.

Check

Name two fields that belong in a model-call log and one that does not.

Show the answer

Belong: model id and token counts, or latency and status. Does not: the API key, or a private document you have no approval to store.

This room pins the OpenTelemetry GenAI names this lab will use, treats cost and latency as worksheets instead of slogans, and keeps the enforcement of a cap in the host.</p><h3>01Executive summary</h3><ul><li>This lab pins the OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic-conventions repository at commit <code>4e8a2812139b2a999d959e3650e24dfc64e21943</code>, dated 2026-10-13. On that tree, <code>gen_ai.operation.name</code> is Development and includes <code>chat</code>, <code>embeddings</code>, <code>execute_tool</code>, and <code>retrieval</code>. [cite:1]</li><li>The public registry page says the GenAI attributes have moved. Cite the commit when you need a frozen tree. Do not treat an example value as a vendor quota. [cite:2]</li><li>LangChain’s overview points at LangSmith to trace, debug, and evaluate. It does not publish a numeric LangSmith quota. Check LangSmith’s own limits page for the plan you pay for. Quotas vary by plan, which is why the overview is not a number. [cite:3]</li><li>Cost figures below are the OpenAI pricing page fetched 2026-10-14, used as arithmetic inputs. They are not a forecast for your tenant. Short context on that page means at most 272k input tokens. [cite:4]</li><li>A latency budget is a worksheet of hops. Universal millisecond targets stay marked. OWASP LLM10 names unbounded consumption: tokens, loops, and retries without a ceiling you set. [cite:5]</li></ul><aside class="callout note"><h3>Why it matters for the lab engineer</h3><p>the lab engineer is fictional. The incident he is practicing for is a Tuesday where the bot is “slow” and “expensive” and nobody can say which hop moved. A single alert called voice latency hides a retry loop. A single number called cost-per-call hides a change in model id. This room is the habit of splitting the trace, the bill, and the guardrail before anyone tunes a prompt.</p></aside><h3>02Architecture</h3><p>One turn becomes four records: a trace, a cost line, a hop time, and an allow or deny.</p><p>Diagram: Request, guardrail, model or tool, trace, and budget worksheet in one path</p><p>The picture is the production path, not the notebook. A request hits a guardrail you wrote: size, identity, and whether this bot may call this tool. Then a model or a tool runs. The trace records which operation name you used. The worksheet adds the tokens and the milliseconds you actually measured. Nothing in the diagram is a SaaS quota. If a vendor’s dashboard disagrees with the span, the span is what you can diff. The dashboard is a view.</p><p>Retrieval, the model, and the tool are different spans. A retry is another span, not a note in the first one.</p><p>Diagram: Caller, guardrail, retriever, model, and tool with separate spans</p><p>Three operation names from the pinned tree are enough to tell this story: <code>retrieval</code>, <code>chat</code>, and <code>execute_tool</code>. Embeddings are the fourth when you are building the index rather than answering. If your trace uses one name for all four, you cannot answer the page that woke you up. [cite:1]</p><h3>03Deep dive</h3><p>LLMOps, in this room, means the work after a demo already answers one question. You have to know what ran, what it cost, how long each hop took, and what was forbidden. T5-R01 owns the golden set and the waiver. This room owns the production record those evals should be able to join. A green nightly job that cannot be joined to a trace id is a lab result. It is not an incident tool.</p><h3>Pin the attribute names</h3><p>OpenTelemetry’s GenAI registry page, fetched 2026-10-14, tells you the attributes have moved and points at the semantic-conventions-genai repository. Moving attributes are a reason to pin a commit, not a reason to stop tracing. The commit this lab pins is <code>4e8a2812139b2a999d959e3650e24dfc64e21943</code>. The date on that commit is 2026-10-13. Read the commit message before you tell a review board that “the spec changed.” The message is a dependency bump. The attribute list you are allowed to cite is the list on that tree, not a list you remember from a slide. [cite:1] [cite:2]</p><p>On that tree, <code>gen_ai.operation.name</code> is marked Development. The values this room will repeat are <code>chat</code>, <code>embeddings</code>, <code>execute_tool</code>, and <code>retrieval</code>. Development means the name can still move. Pinning the commit means your dashboards and your docs name the same tree. It does not freeze the upstream project. When you move the pin, you diff the attribute file and you change the dashboard in the same change. A dashboard that queries a name the new tree removed will go blank and someone will say tracing is broken. The query is what broke.</p><aside class="callout note"><h3>Gotcha</h3><p>LangSmith, Langfuse, and Phoenix are not the same sentence. LangChain’s overview, fetched 2026-10-14, says LangSmith is how you trace, debug, and evaluate agents built there. It does not describe Langfuse or Phoenix, and it does not give a numeric quota. Do not invent a span cap, a seat count, or a retention period for a product the page did not quantify. If you need a number, open that product’s page and date the fetch. [cite:3]</p></aside><div class="table-wrap"><table><thead><tr><th>Name on the pinned tree</th><th>Use it when</th><th>Do not use it when</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td><code>chat</code></td><td>A model completion that is the reply or the tool decision</td><td>You really did a retrieval and want the time blamed on the model</td></tr><tr><td><code>embeddings</code></td><td>You are embedding a query or a document</td><td>You are only reading neighbors that were embedded last week</td></tr><tr><td><code>retrieval</code></td><td>The index lookup, including a miss</td><td>The subsequent generation. That is chat.</td></tr><tr><td><code>execute_tool</code></td><td>The host ran a tool, including a refusal you still record</td><td>The model merely proposed a call that you dropped</td></tr></tbody></table></div><p>A proposal that you refuse is still worth a span, or at least a log line, because the incident is often “the model asked.” Mark the outcome as denied. Do not emit <code>execute_tool</code> for a call that never left the process if your convention says the name means the tool ran. Pick one and document it next to the pin. The pinned tree will not know your deny reason. That attribute is local. Write it down so the next reader does not invent <code>gen_ai.denied</code> and think it is standard.</p><h3>What a trace must carry</h3><p>Minimum fields this room will defend, without claiming they are all in the GenAI registry: trace id, model id, prompt hash, operation name from the pinned list, token counts if the API returned them, tool name if a tool was involved, allow or deny, and a redaction flag. The prompt hash is the instruction text you versioned, not the caller’s paragraph. Store the caller’s paragraph only if the retention decision says so. GDPR Article 5(1)(e) says no longer than necessary. This lab’s default is not to store the caller’s paragraph. [cite:11] The flag can still be false by default in the lab, which is the safe side of an unknown policy.</p><p>Join keys are how evals become operations. T5-R01’s case id should be able to appear on a span when you are replaying a golden case, and it should be absent on live traffic unless you have decided that production sampling is allowed to keep the text. Online eval is not a reason to keep raw audio. The voice room already says that. This room repeats it because the tracing vendor’s default retention is exactly the kind of number people paste from a blog. We do not have that number. [cite:3]</p><p>Sampling of traces is a budget control and a blind spot. If you keep one percent of successes and one hundred percent of errors, you can debug incidents and you cannot compute a true average cost from the trace store alone. Cost should come from the provider’s usage export or from a counter you increment on every call, not only on sampled spans. Write that down in the worksheet. A sampled trace is a story. An unsampled counter is the bill’s cousin.</p><h3>Cost is a worksheet</h3><p>The OpenAI pricing page fetched 2026-10-14 is the source for the figures in this section. Standard short context means at most 272k input tokens. Above that, the page has different rates for the models it lists as having a long-context price. Do not apply the short-context number to a 300k prompt and call it conservative. You would be using the wrong row. [cite:4]</p><div class="table-wrap"><table><thead><tr><th>Row on the page fetched 2026-10-14</th><th>Figure</th><th>How this room uses it</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>gpt-4o-mini, standard</td><td>$0.15 input and $0.60 output per 1M tokens</td><td>Arithmetic example only. Re-fetch before a budget meeting.</td></tr><tr><td>gpt-6-luna, standard short context</td><td>$0.10 input and $0.50 output per 1M tokens</td><td>Same. Short context means at most 272k input tokens.</td></tr><tr><td>text-embedding-3-small</td><td>$0.02 per 1M tokens</td><td>Index builds and query embeddings. Not the chat row.</td></tr><tr><td>text-embedding-3-large</td><td>$0.13 per 1M tokens</td><td>Do not mix this vector with a small index. T3.</td></tr><tr><td>Regional processing uplift</td><td>10% for eligible models released on or after 5 March 2026</td><td>Eligibility is a page check. This room does not decide it for you.</td></tr></tbody></table></div><p>A worksheet line is tokens in, tokens out, the row you believe applies, and the product. Example, not a bill: 2,000 input tokens and 500 output tokens on the gpt-4o-mini standard row is 2,000/1,000,000 times $0.15 plus 500/1,000,000 times $0.60. That is a fraction of a cent. It becomes a budget only when you multiply by calls per day and add retries. The retry is the usual missing term. A client that retries twice has tripled the line if all three calls were billed. Your trace should show three chat spans or one span plus a retry count you trust. A single span with a note that says “retried” will be dropped by the next person who sums spans.</p><p>Tool loops re-send context. T2-R03 already said the next call includes the tool result. The cost worksheet has to count that second chat span. People budget the first completion and forget the follow-up that actually speaks to the caller. Embeddings are a separate line. Re-embedding a corpus because someone changed models is an index event, not a per-call event, and it belongs on the change ticket. Query embeddings belong on the request. Mixing them produces a scary graph on the day you reindex and a false alarm.</p><p>The regional-processing uplift is a ten percent addition for eligible models released on or after 5 March 2026, on the page this room fetched. “Eligible” is the word that stops you from adding ten percent to every row in the spreadsheet. If you cannot show the eligibility line for the model id you serve, the uplift cell in the worksheet stays blank and marked, not filled with a guess. A blank cell is a better budget than a confident wrong one. [cite:4]</p><aside class="callout note"><h3>Cache and batch are different rows</h3><p>The same pricing page has cached-input and batch prices for some models. A worksheet that uses the standard output price for a cached prefix will overstate the bill, and one that assumes every token was cached will understate it. Record whether the API reported cached tokens. If it did not, do not invent a cache hit rate. Batch is a different product shape, not a discount you apply in your head to a realtime call.</p></aside><h3>Latency is a sum of hops</h3><p>Write the hops before you write a target. For a text bot: guardrail, retrieval, chat, tool, second chat. For a voice bot, add the media edge, and do not copy a millisecond from a browser demo. T7-R01 keeps universal end-to-end targets marked because they are measurements. This room does not sneak a number in through the back door. A budget can still say “page someone when the tool hop’s p95 doubles week over week” without saying the p95 must be 200 milliseconds. The doubling is a rule about your own history. The 200 is a costume. [cite:5]</p><p>OpenAI’s Realtime guide uses “low latency” as an adjective. The VAD guide’s sample uses 300 milliseconds of prefix padding and 500 milliseconds of silence. Those are example fields, already cited in T7-R01. They are not the contact-center budget. If a dashboard labels a line “VAD 500” as if it were a service-level objective, delete the label. Put the example in a footnote on the config, and put the measured endpointing time in the hop table. [cite:6]</p><p>Guardrail time counts. A regex pass is small. A second model call that “checks safety” is another chat span and another bill, and it can be slower than the answer. If you add a judge model, it goes on the worksheet as its own row with its own model id. NIST’s Measure function is test before deployment and regularly in operation. A judge that you do not time will be the hop that surprises you, and a judge that shares the generator’s tastes can approve the failure T5-R01 already warned about. The operational version of that warning is: the judge span is visible, and money cases are not gated by the judge alone. [cite:7]</p><h3>Guardrails are controls, not a product name</h3><p>This room uses guardrail to mean a control you can point at in code or in a gateway config you have read. It does not name a vendor’s guardrail SKU, because that SKU’s settings were not fetched. The controls that are already grounded in this lab are: a size cap on input, a tool allow-list per bot, a host check before a side effect, a schema for shape on the models the structured-outputs guide names, and a stop condition on loops. OWASP LLM10 is unbounded consumption. LLM06 is excessive agency. LLM01 is injection, which a schema does not fix. You can have all three controls and still be injected. You cannot have none of them and call the bot guarded. [cite:5] [cite:8]</p><p>Input size is the cheapest ceiling. Reject, or summarize with a traced summarizer, when the caller pastes a book. The token-counting guide’s point, already used in T7, is that output caps include tokens you may not see. A small <code>max_output_tokens</code> can end a reply before the caller hears anything. That is a guardrail with a failure mode. Record the finish reason. If the reason is the cap, the incident is the cap, not “the model was rude.” [cite:9]</p><p>Loop ceilings are the second cheapest. A tool loop without a maximum number of steps will follow a confused model until the bill does. Pick a number for your bot, write it next to the prompt hash, and fail the turn when you hit it. The number is yours. This room will not pretend there is a universal step count. Three tool rounds is a common lab choice and not a standard. Mark any “industry standard step count” as something you will not cite. The control is that a number exists and is enforced in the host, not in a sentence the model can be talked out of.</p><p>Output handling is LLM05. Do not pass model text into a shell, a SQL string, or a case-note template without an allow-list of fields. A structured object makes this easier and does not finish it. T2-R03’s checker still runs. From the ops side, the deny is a metric. Count denies. A sudden drop in denies can mean the check was deployed out of the path. A sudden spike can mean a bad article or an attack. Both are pages. Neither is a reason to delete the check to make the graph calm. [cite:5]</p><h3>Budgets, alerts, and the thing you will not page on</h3><p>Page on a hop you can name. “Model quality dropped” is not a hop. A faithfulness fail on the golden set is an eval alert, owned by T5-R01, and it can block a deploy. A p95 tool duration that doubled is an ops alert, and it can page. A one-minute blip on a sampled trace is a story you read in the morning. Write the difference into the alert catalog so the on-call rotation does not learn it during the blip.</p><p>Cost alerts need a window and a baseline. “More than yesterday” pages every Monday. Use a weekly baseline or a trailing weekday, and exclude the reindex job or you will page the person who did the job you asked for. The alert body should contain the model id and the operation name. An alert that says “OpenAI spend” when the spike was embeddings will send the on-call into the chat prompts. The table above is the difference.</p><p>Error budgets for quality are waivers with an expiry, which T5-R01 and T8 already require.
